analysis.one_liner: Gives Senate candidates free TV time and discounted ads if they accept campaign spending limits.
analysis.headline: Five senators sponsored the bill and the Senate Rules Committee held six hearings in 1996, but it never came to a vote in committee or on the floor and died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a voluntary system for Senate campaigns: candidates who filed certified agreements to keep spending under set limits would earn benefits, including 30 minutes of free broadcast time, TV ads at up to half off the station's lowest rate, and reduced postage. It would also cap how much of their own money candidates and their families could spend, raise contribution limits for opponents of big self-funders, ban spending campaign donations on personal expenses, and tighten disclosure rules on political ads.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters would get Senate campaigns financed less by unlimited personal fortunes and with clearer disclosure of who is paying for ads. Candidates who accept the limits would receive free airtime, discounted ad rates, and cheaper mailings, making it easier to run for Senate without relying on large donors.

how_it_helps.text: Candidates who agree to the spending limits receive 30 minutes of free broadcast time in their state, TV advertising rates no higher than 50% of the station's lowest charge in the final 30 and 60 days, and reduced postage rates for a set volume of mail.
A participating candidate's own spending — personal funds plus family funds and loans — would be capped at the lesser of $250,000 or 10% of the general election limit.

If a candidate declares intent to spend more than $250,000 of personal or family money, opponents' individual contribution limits rise from $1,000 to $5,000, and if the self-funder spends more than $1 million, the limit on opponents' contributions is removed entirely.
Campaign funds could no longer be used for inherently personal purposes such as mortgage payments, clothing, country club memberships, or vacations.
Broadcast and cable political ads would have to carry an on-screen and spoken statement identifying who approved or paid for the message, and print ads would need a clearly readable sponsorship box.

analysis.who_pays: Broadcasters would give up free airtime and sell candidate ads at deep discounts; cable systems would face license revocation for denying candidates access; wealthy self-financing candidates and their families would be limited; and incumbents could no longer spend campaign donations on personal expenses.

drawbacks.text: The general election spending cap starts at $5.5 million and the primary cap at $2.75 million — figures well below what Senate races in large, expensive media states actually cost, so candidates in those states would have to run on far less money than current campaigns spend.

The system is voluntary and works by rewarding compliance with broadcast and postage benefits rather than mandating limits, so candidates who refuse the deal can spend without restriction — the same structural weakness that led courts to strike down mandatory spending limits in campaigns.
Penalizing a self-funding candidate by raising the opponent's contribution limits shifts the burden onto donors rather than reducing money in the race overall.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks a real problem — the escalating cost of Senate campaigns and the role of personal fortunes — and adds genuine transparency rules. But it is built entirely on voluntary compliance sweetened with broadcast discounts, and its spending caps are low enough that serious candidates in big states might rationally decline the deal, leaving the system with limited reach. It would still have imposed real accountability on personal use of campaign funds and ad disclosure even if the spending limits underperformed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Rules Committee, which held hearings on it six times between February and May 1996, but the committee never voted to send it to the floor and the 104th Congress ended with the bill dead.

narrative.text: Sen. Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on November 3, 1995, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration.
Four Democratic senators signed on as cosponsors.
The Rules Committee held hearings on the bill on six dates between February 1 and May 15, 1996, printed as S.Hrg. 104-542.
After the last hearing on May 15, 1996, no further action was taken — no committee markup or vote, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Senate incumbents and the existing campaign money system came out ahead: no spending limits, no restriction on personal use of campaign funds, and no free-airtime obligations on broadcasters were enacted. Broadcast television stations kept selling candidate ads at full rates.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
for.what_they_did: Held six hearings on the bill between February and May 1996 (S.Hrg. 104-542).

against.name: Sen. John Warner
against.role: Chair, Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that held hearings but never reported the bill out, keeping it from a Senate floor vote.

against.name: Broadcast television and cable station owners
against.role: Licensed broadcasters who would bear the costs of free airtime and discounted rates
against.what_they_did: Broadcasters have historically opposed mandates for free candidate airtime and discounted ad rates; the bill would have required them to provide 30 minutes of free time and sell ads at up to half off their lowest rates.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes occurred, but all five sponsors were Democrats in a Senate controlled by a 53-seat Republican majority, and the bill never advanced past the Republican-chaired Rules Committee.

industries.note: Eligible candidates would get 30 minutes of free airtime per station and pay no more than half the lowest ad rate in the final month or two of the campaign, cutting directly into stations' most lucrative political-ad revenue. Stations could also lose licenses for denying candidates access.

The bill extends the rule allowing license revocation for denying candidates reasonable access to cable systems, requiring cable operators to sell candidate time on the same terms as their most favored advertiser.

industries.industry: Wealthy individuals who self-fund Senate campaigns
industries.note: Candidates who take the limits could spend at most $250,000 of personal and family money, and any candidate spending more than $250,000 of own funds would trigger higher contribution limits for opponents. The burden falls on the wealthiest candidates and their donors.

industries.industry: Direct mail and political advertising firms
industries.note: Eligible candidates get reduced postage for a volume of mail set by state population, subsidizing mail vendors, while new sponsorship-disclosure and 'stand by your ad' requirements add compliance work to every political ad.
